items.title: Getting Dressed as a Medieval Queen
items.description:
Medieval stories and fairy-tales show us long gowns, big sleeves, and tall conical hats for princesses. But how accurate is this? What did medieval women really wear?

Burgundy was considered one of the most fashionable places in Europe in the 14th Century, and many medieval women in the 1500s wore the extravagant Burgundian gown. It is likely that some of the queens and noble women who stayed at the Tower of London dressed in this style.

global_silver_linings.reason: There's a gentle comfort in watching a generation of parents choose ease and practicality over pressure — prioritising being present with their kids over keeping up appearances. Comfy clothes as a cultural statement might sound small, but it signals a real shift toward self-acceptance.

discovery_articles.title: The Iconic Watts Towers in Los Angeles Will Get a $22 Million Campus Expansion Ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics
discovery_articles.snippet: Five acres of green space will surround the 17-structure landmark, a folk art masterpiece that an Italian immigrant built over the course of three decades
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Sabato Rodia, a tile setter with no formal art training, spent 33 years weaving broken glass, seashells, and ceramic shards into towers that now stand as one of America's most extraordinary folk art monuments — built entirely alone, then quietly deeded to a neighbor before he walked away and never returned. There's something achingly human about a man pouring three decades into a dream, then simply leaving it behind.

discovery_articles.title: Archaeologists Discover Two Thumbnail-Size Bird Sculptures Carved From Mammoth Ivory 40,000 Years Ago
discovery_articles.snippet: Measuring less than an inch long, the figurines were buried beneath Germany's Hohle Fels Cave, where some of the world's oldest known figurative artworks have been found
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Someone 40,000 years ago — before written language, before cities, before almost everything we call civilization — sat down and carved a bird smaller than your thumbnail from mammoth ivory with enough care to capture the curve of a wing. The urge to make something beautiful and precise is apparently as old as us.

featured_read.title: The Log from the Sea of Cortez: John Steinbeck’s Forgotten Masterpiece on How to Think and the Art of Seeing the Pattern Beyond the Particular
featured_read.snippet: "Everything impinges on everything else... Everything is potentially everywhere."
featured_read.blurb: Steinbeck, better known for Okies and dustbowls, turns out to have written one of the most quietly radical defenses of scientific wonder ever put to paper — and this essay traces exactly how he learned to look past the specimen in the jar to the living web it came from. Set aside the half-hour and let it rearrange the way you notice things.

The garden is at that satisfying, slightly shaggy peak where abundance and gentle decline are perfectly intertwined.
